26-036.r: Double Dome → Sikandar Lodi; Octagonal Tomb → Sher Shah; True Arch Tomb → Balban; Gol Gumbad → Muhammad Adil Shah.
26-036.t: Don't confuse Balban's tomb (true arch) with Sikandar Lodi's tomb (double dome).

26-037.r: Jahaj Mahal, Mandu → built in the period of Ghiyasuddin Khalji; there is no 'Jantar Mahal' in Mandu.
26-037.c: Answer not printed: M.P. P.S.C. deleted the question because no Jantar Mahal exists in Mandu.

26-039.r: Gujari Mahal → built by Raja Man Singh Tomar between 1486-1516 A.D.

26-040.r: Adina Masjid → Pandua (West Bengal), built 1364-1374 by Sikandar Shah, not Mandu; Lal Darwaza Masjid → Jaunpur; Dakhil Darwaza → Gaour; Tin Darwaza → Ahmedabad.

26-041.r: Atala Devi Masjid → Ibrahim Shah Sharqi; Chhota Sona Masjid → Wali Muhammad; Qadam Rasul → Nusrat Shah; Adina Masjid, Pandua → Sikandar Shah.

26-042.r: Polygars (Palaiyakkarar) → territorial administrative and military governors appointed by the Nayaka rulers of South India, 16th-18th centuries.

27-001.r: Bhakti movement → started by Vaishnava Alvar saints (with Shaiva Nayanars); began in the Dravida region and spread north from the 13th-14th centuries.

27-002.r: Bhakti reborn in 15th-16th century AD → Kabir, Tulsi, Nanak, Sur, Mirabai; earlier Shankaracharya (8th century) gave Advaitavada against Buddhism's influence.

27-003.r: Common belief of Buddha and Mirabai → the world is full of sorrow (sorrow is the first of Buddhism's Four Arya Truths).

27-004.r: 'Let no man ask a man's sect or caste' → dictum of Ramananda; his pupils came from all castes, religions and sects.

27-005.r: Common feature of all Bhakti saints → verses in regional and local languages that their followers easily understood.

27-006.r: Sufi practices → meditation and breath control, severe ascetic exercises in a lonely place, holy songs (Sama) to arouse ecstasy; all three correct.

27-007.r: Vaishnavism in Kamarupa (Assam) → Shankaradeva, founder of Ekasarana sect (Vaishnava cult); devotion to one deity Krishna; opposed rituals and idolatry.

27-009.r: Vaishnavism in Assam and Cooch Behar → introduced by Shankaradeva.

27-010.r: Ramanujacharya → Vishishtadvaita (non-duality qualified by attributes); an earliest propagator of the Bhakti Movement.

27-011.r: Shuddha Advaitavada (pure non-dualism) → Vallabhacharya, founder of the Vallabha sect; developed the views of Vishnuswami.

27-012.r: Vallabhacharya → born in the forest of Champaranya (Vikram Samvat 1535); founded Krishna-centred Pushti sect and Suddha Advaita philosophy.

27-013.r: Advaita → Shankaracharya; Vishishtadvaita → Ramanujacharya; Dvaita → Madhvacharya; Dvaitadvaita → Nimbarkacharya.

27-014.r: Vallabhacharya → Pushtimarg; Ramanuj → Vishishtadvaita; Madhvacharya → Dvaitavada; Shankar → Advaitavada.

27-015.r: Ramanuja → Vishishtadvaita; Madhavacharya → Dvaita; Nimbarka → Dvaitadvaita; Vallabhacharya → Suddhadvait.

27-016.r: Wrong: Madhvacharya (Dvaita) followed Saguna Bhakti, not Nirguna; correct: Vallabhacharya → Pushtimarg, Nimbarka → Dvaitadvaita, Ramananda → Rama Bhakti.

27-017.r: Bijak → Kabir's works (Kabirpanthi scripture), not Dadu Dayal; Pushtimarg → Vallabhacharya (Shuddha Advaita), not Madhvacharya; both statements wrong.

27-018.r: First Bhakti saint to use Hindi → Ramananda (born 1299 A.D., Prayag, Kanyakubja Brahmin); spread worship of Rama and Sita among the masses.

27-019.r: Born in Prayag → Ramananda; Raidas → Varanasi; Tulsidas → Chitrakoot (Rajapur); Kumbhandas → Mathura.

27-020.r: Kabir → most prominent of the 12 disciples of Ramananda; raised by weaver couple Neeru and Neema near Varanasi.

27-021.r: Bijak → collection of Kabir's couplets; main religious text of the Kabirpanthi sect.

27-022.r: 'Pothi Padh Padh Jag Mua, Pandit Bhaya Na Koye, Dhai Akhar Prem Ka, Padhe So Pandit Hoye' → Kabir Das.

27-023.r: Dialogues between Kabir and Dharamdas → Amarmul (Anurag Sagar); Sakhi, Sabad and Ramaini are Kabir's own compositions.

27-024.r: Saint poet Malukdas → born 1574 A.D. at Kada (Kaushambi, Uttar Pradesh), son of Lala Sunder Das Khatri.

27-025.r: Guru Ghasidas (born December 1756, Giraudpuri, Chhattisgarh) → parents Mahangudas (Mahangu) and Amarautin.

27-026.r: Chronology → Shankaracharya (8th century) – Ramanuja (1017-1137 A.D.) – Chaitanya (1486-1533 A.D.).

27-027.r: Chronology → Kabir (1398-1518) – Guru Nanak (1469-1539) – Chaitanya (1486-1533) – Mirabai (1498-1546).

27-028.r: Jyotirlingas of Shiva → 12, e.g. Somnath (Gujarat), Kedarnath, Kashi Vishwanath, Vaidyanath (Deoghar), Mahakaleshwara (Ujjain), Omkareshwar (Narmada).

27-029.r: Followers of Ramanuja → Vaishnava; his philosophy → Vishishtadvaita.

27-030.r: Guru Nanak → born at Nankana (Pakistan), April 15, 1469, Khatri family; died 1539 at Derababa Nanak (Kartarpur); worshipped Nirakar Brahma.

27-031.r: Guru Nanak (1469-1539) founded Sikh religion in the reign of Sikandar Lodi (1489-1517 A.D.); believed in one formless God (Ik Onkar).

27-032.r: 'God knows man's virtues and inquires not his caste' → Guru Nanak; he started the free community kitchen 'Guru Ka Langar'.

27-033.r: Mirabai (daughter of Ratan Singh Rathore of Merta; wife of Bhojraj, son of Rana Sanga) → contemporary of Tulsidas, Guru Nanak and Chaitanya, not Ramakrishna.
27-033.c: Answer not printed: the explanation makes three options (Tulsidas, Chaitanya, Guru Nanak) contemporaries of Mirabai.

27-037.r: Chronology → Namdev – Kabir – Guru Nanak – Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

27-038.r: Namdev → Bhakti saint most influenced by Islam; born 1270 A.D. at Narsi (Maharashtra); disciple of Vishoba Khechar; Varakari sect; opposed idolatry.

27-039.r: Preaching when Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi (Panipat, 1526) → only Guru Nanak (1469-1539); Dadu Dayal 1544-1603; Tyagaraja 1767-1847.

27-040.r: Namdev → Tailor; Kabir → Weaver; Ravidas → Cobbler; Sena → Barber.

27-041.r: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu → Vaishnava sect (Krishna devotion); born in Nadia (West Bengal); childhood name Nimai; parents Jagannath Mishra and Shachi Devi.

27-042.r: Tulsidas → contemporary of Akbar and Jahangir; wrote Ramcharitmanas and Vinay Patrika; lived mostly in Banaras, no link with the court.

27-043.r: Ramcharitmanas → written by Goswami Tulsidas in Awadhi language.

27-044.r: Tulsidas wrote Gitavali, Kavitavali and Vinay Patrika; Sahitya Ratna is not his work.

27-046.r: Geetavali, Vinay Patrika, Kavitavali → Tulsidas; Sahitya Lahari → Surdas.
27-046.t: Don't confuse Surdas's Sahitya Lahari with Tulsidas's Geetavali or Kavitavali.

27-047.r: Tulsidas → born at Rajapur village, Chitrakoot district (not Banda); wife Ratnawali (not Geetawali); both statements wrong.

27-048.r: Rasik Priya → Acharya Keshavdas (also Ramchandrika, Kavi Priya), not Raskhan; Dhruvadas → Bhagat Namawali; Nabhadas → Bhaktamal; Usman → Chitrawali.

27-049.r: Namdev → saint of the Varkari sect; Visoba Khechar taught him mystic life.

27-050.r: Varkari sect main seat → Pandharpur (Solapur, Maharashtra) on River Chandrabhaga (Bhima); Varkaris worship Vitthal, a form of Krishna.

27-051.r: Tukaram (1608-1650 A.D.) → contemporary of Jahangir (1605-1627) and Shahjahan (1628-1658); Jahangir chosen as Shahjahan is not an option.

27-052.r: Not a Bhakti proponent → Nagarjuna, founder of 'Nihilism' (first/second centuries A.D.); Tukaram, Tyagaraja and Vallabhacharya were medieval Bhakti saints.

27-053.r: Kabir → Swami Ramananda; Amir Khusrau → Nizamuddin Auliya; Surdas → Vallabhacharya; Mardana → Guru Nanak (disciple → guru).

27-054.r: Sanskrit music works translated into Persian (rulers' interest, e.g. Firuz Tughluq, Sikandar Lodi); early Chishtis loved 'sama'; both true, R not the explanation.

27-055.r: Chishtia order → founded at Chishti Sharif (Afghanistan) by Abu Ishaq Shami and Khwaja Abu Ahmad Abdal; brought to India by Muinuddin Chishti (came 1192, Ajmer, died 1236).
27-055.t: Founder abroad (Abu Ishaq Shami / Abu Abdal) differs from founder in India (Muinuddin Chishti).

27-059.r: Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti → disciple of Khwaja Usman Haruni (at Nishapur); born in Sijistan, 1138-39 A.D.

27-061.r: First Maratha chief to offer nazr (gift) at Muinuddin Chishti's Dargah, Ajmer → Raja Sahu, grandson of Shivaji.

27-062.r: Nizamuddin Auliya → disciple of Baba Farid (Fariduddin Ganj-i-Shakar), born in Multan district; Alauddin Sabir Kaliyari was another disciple of Baba Farid.

27-063.r: Dargah of Shaikh Nizamuddin Auliya → Delhi; he died 1325 AD, buried at Ghiyaspur; a main disciple of Baba Farid with Alauddin Sabir.

27-064.r: Chishti order → founded by Khwaja Abu Ishaq Shami of Syria, named after Chist (Chishti Sharif, Afghanistan), not a village in Ajmer; brought to India by Muinuddin Chishti (1192).

27-065.r: Muinuddin Chishti → introduced the Chishti order in India; held that devotional music is one way to come closer to God.

27-066.r: Shaikh Abdul Jilani → founded the Qadiri order, not Chishti; Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, Moinuddin and Nizamuddin Auliya were Chishti saints.

27-067.r: 'Sadi of India' (Sadi-i Hind) → Amir Hasan-i-Dehlavi, for his great Ghazals.
27-067.t: Don't confuse Amir Hasan with Amir Khusrau.

27-068.r: Nizamuddin Auliya ('Mehboob-i-Ilahi') → refused audience to Alauddin Khalji ('two doors in my home'); saw over seven Sultans, never visited their court.

27-071.r: Nizamuddin Auliya → most reputed disciple of Shaikh Farid; saw over seven Delhi Sultans; titles 'Mehboob-i-Ilahi' (Favourite of God), 'Sultan-ul-Mashaikh' (King of Saints).

27-072.r: Baba Farid (Fariduddin Ganj-i-Shakar, Chishti) → his compositions are in the Guru Granth Sahib (Adi Granth); centres Hansi and Ajodhan.

27-073.r: Shaikh Salim Chishti ('Shaikh-ul-Hind') → lived at Sikri, 37 km from Agra, later developed by Akbar as Fatehpur Sikri.

27-075.r: 'Chirag-i-Delhi' → Shaikh Nasiruddin Mahmud, disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya.

27-076.r: Chiragh-i-Delhi → Nasiruddin Mahmud; not Shaikh Nizamuddin, Fariduddin Masud or Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki.

27-077.r: Nizamuddin Auliya → Delhi (born Badayun, UP; lived with Baba Farid at Ajodhan), not Multan; Moinuddin Chishti → Ajmer; Burhanuddin Gharib → Daulatabad; Mohammad Hussaini → Gulbarga.

27-078.r: Muinuddin Chishti → Chishtiya; Ahmad Sirhindi → Naqshbandiya; Dara Shukoh → Qadiriya; Shaikh Shahabuddin → Suhrawardiya.

27-079.r: True: Nasiruddin Chirag-i-Dehlavi was Nizamuddin Auliya's disciple; Niamatullah and Makhdum Muhammad Jilani brought the Qadiri order. False: Ahmad Sirhindi (Akbar, Jahangir), Salim Chishti (Akbar).

27-080.r: Hath Yog → practised by Nathpanthis (founder Guru Matsyendranath); later adopted by Sufis, e.g. Muhammad Ghaus's 'Bahar-Al-Hayat'; both true.

27-081.r: Both false: Nimbarka (Dvaitadvaita) lived around 11th-12th century, not under Akbar; Ahmad Sirhindi (1564-1624) came after Kabir (1398-1518).

27-082.r: Sufi saints → Nizamuddin Auliya and Muinuddin Chishti (Chishti order); Rahim and Raskhan were medieval Hindi poets.

27-083.r: Sufi order against music → Naqshbandiya, founded by Bahauddin Naqshband (14th century); Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi (Mujaddid) belonged to it.
27-083.t: Chishtis loved music (sama); Naqshbandis opposed it.

27-084.r: Most orthodox Sufi order → Naqshbandi; founded by Baha-ud-Din Naqshband (14th century), popularised in India by Babur; rigid adherence to Shariat.
27-084.c: Book gives (c) Naqshbandi but notes the JPSC official key gave (b) Suhrawardi.

27-085.r: Incorrect pair → Auliya–Madhya Pradesh: Auliya is Nizamuddin's title (Delhi), not an order; Chishti → Delhi and Doab; Suhrawardi → Sindh; Firdausi → Bihar.

27-086.r: Firdausia (Firdousi) Silsila → founded in Bihar; chief Sufi Sheikh Sharfuddin Yahya Maneri.

27-087.r: Shah Muhammad Ghaus (Shattari order) → regarded Krishna as an Auliya; close to Humayun and Tansen; translated 'Amritkund' as 'Bahar-ul-Hayat'.

27-088.r: Shaikh Bahauddin Zakaria → started the Suhrawardi order in India.

27-089.r: Suhrawardi order → came to India with the Chishtis but was confined mainly to Punjab, Multan and Sindh; established by Baha-Ud-Din Zakariya.
27-089.h: S for Suhrawardi, S for Sindh.

27-090.r: Not Sufi → Ulema (scholars of Islamic religious law); Khanqah = Sufi residence, Sama = Sufi music gathering, Shaikh = Sufi guide.

27-091.r: Prem Vatika (Braj, on Krishna's life) → Raskhan (real name Sayyid Ibrahim); he also wrote 'Sujan Raskhan'.

27-092.r: Amir Khusrau (Abul Hasan Yaminuddin Khusrau) → poet, not in the Bhakti Movement; works Qiran-us-Sadain, Miftah-ul-Futuh, Nuh Sipihr, Ashiqa, Khazain-ul-Futuh.

27-093.r: Barahmasa → Malik Muhammad Jayasi, part of his Padmavat; other works Akharavat and Aakhiri Kalaam.

27-094.r: Mulla Daud → Chandayan; Damodar Kavi → Padmavati Katha; Somnath → Rag Vibodh; Amir Khusrau → Ashiqa.

27-095.r: Annual fair at tomb of Sufi Haji Waris Ali Shah → Dewa Sharif, Barabanki (Uttar Pradesh).

27-096.r: Jesus Christ → born in Bethlehem (south of Jerusalem).

27-097.r: Easter → celebrates the Resurrection of Jesus Christ on the third day after his crucifixion.

27-098.r: Saint Francis of Assisi (1181/82-1226 A.D.) → famous for his love of animals and birds.

27-099.r: Good Friday → remembers the crucifixion (sacrificial death) of Jesus Christ, hanged on a Friday.

28-001.r: Alam Khan → uncle of Ibrahim Lodi and pretender to the Delhi throne, invited Babur; Daulat Khan also invited Babur, sending his son Dilawar Khan.
28-001.t: Dilawar Khan was Daulat Khan's son, not Alam Khan's.

28-003.r: Mughal rulers → Chagatai Turks, named after Genghis Khan's second son, ruler of Central Asia and Turkistan.

28-004.r: Battle of Sar-e-Pul → Shaybani Khan defeated Babur (invaded Ferghana 1501, took Samarqand), using the Tulughma technique.

28-005.r: Ottoman system of war in India → Babur at First Battle of Panipat (1526): artillery under Ali Quli, Tulughma and Araba tactics.

28-006.r: First Battle of Panipat → Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi, April 21, 1526; Ibrahim Lodi killed; area up to Delhi and Agra came under Babur.

28-007.r: Main reason for Babur's victory at Panipat (21 April 1526) → his skilled warfare; his army was smaller than Ibrahim Lodi's.

28-008.r: Reason for Babur's victory over Ibrahim Lodi (this question) → skilled commandants.
28-008.t: Same battle, different keys: 'skilled warfare' in one paper, 'skilled commandant' here; read the options.

28-009.r: Artillery first used in India → First Battle of Panipat (1526, Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi); Babur first used guns at Bajaur (1519); artillery Ustad Ali Quli, gunners Mustafa.

28-011.r: Babur defeated and killed Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat → 21st April 1526 A.D.; Ibrahim had become Sultan in 1517.

28-012.r: Babur's battles → Panipat 1526 (Ibrahim Lodi), Khanwa 1527 (Rana Sanga), Chanderi 1528 (Medini Rai), Ghaghara 1529 (Afghans); Chanderi was not 1530.
28-012.h: P-K-C-G: Panipat, Khanwa, Chanderi, Ghaghara, one battle a year.

28-014.r: Babur's arrival → set up the Timurid dynasty in India (Timur on father's side, Genghis Khan on mother's); gunpowder was already in India before him.

28-016.r: Babur declared 'Jehad' → Battle of Khanwa (16 March 1527) against Rana Sanga of Mewar; after winning he took the title 'Ghazi'.
28-016.t: Don't confuse Khanwa (Rana Sanga, 1527) with Panipat (Ibrahim Lodi).

28-020.r: Zahiruddin Muhammad → Babur; born February 14, 1483 at Ferghana to Umar Shaikh Mirza; Ferghana throne June 1494, aged 11; founded Mughal empire 1526.

28-021.r: Babur first took the title 'Padshah' → at Kabul, after winning it in 1504, giving up the ancestral title 'Mirza'.

28-022.r: Babur's empire → Kabul, Punjab and modern Uttar Pradesh, not Rajasthan; Badakhshan given to Humayun; Mir Yusuf Ali governor of Lahore.

28-023.r: Mughal whose patience and resolution are a lesson → Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur: lost his father in childhood, yet founded the Mughal Empire.

28-024.r: Hindu states named in Babur Nama → Vijayanagara and Mewar (Rana Sanga).

28-025.r: Babur's memoir Tuzuk-i-Babri (Baburnama) → written in Turkish; the Mughal official language was Persian, not Turki; A true, R false.

28-026.r: Tuzk-e-Babri → written by Babur in Chagatai Turki (Turkish); Turki was not the official language of the Mughal court; A true, R false.

28-028.r: Babri mosque, Ayodhya → believed built by Mir Baqi, a commandant of Babur.

29-001.r: Humayun's half-brothers → Kamran, Askari, Hindal (sons of Babur); not Usman; Humayun = Babur's eldest son, born Kabul 1508, mother Maham Begum.

29-002.r: Humayun's battles in order → Devara/Daurah (1532, Afghans, on Gomati) – Chausa (26 June 1539, lost to Sher Shah) – Kanauj – Sirhind.

29-003.r: Rao-Jaitsi-Ro-Chhanda (Beethu Souza) → Rao Jaitsi of Bikaner defeated Kamran Mirza, sent by Humayun in the 1530s.

29-004.r: Offer to give up Bihar and pay 10 lakh dinars a year if allowed to keep Bengal → Sher Khan to Humayun; Humayun declined.

29-005.r: Battle near Kannauj (17th May 1540) → Shershah defeated Humayun; also called Battle of Bilgram (Hardoi district, U.P.).

29-006.r: Farid Khan (later Sher Shah Suri) → educated at Jaunpur, then famous as 'Siraj-i Hind'; left home for Jaunpur in 1494 AD.

29-007.r: Highly educated medieval ruler → Sher Shah, who completed his formal education at Jaunpur, the centre of learning.

29-008.r: Sher Khan → 'Hazrat-e-Ala' after defeating Nusrat Shah of Bengal; royal title 'Sher Shah' after beating Humayun at Chausa (June 26th, 1539).

29-009.r: Sher Shah Suri's reforms → revenue (Ryotwari, settled directly with peasants), administrative, military and currency; all four; seen as Akbar's forerunner.

29-010.r: First ruler to issue a gold coin after the Delhi Sultanate fell → Humayun; Sher Shah also issued gold coins after him.
29-010.c: Book says the UKPSC key gave (a) Akbar, which it calls wrong.

29-011.r: Humayun's first invasion of Chunar Fort → 1532 AD (four-month siege; Sher Khan accepted his supremacy); Kalinjar 1531; Raisina fort 1535.

29-012.r: Chronology → Daurah (1532) – Chausa (1539) – Kannauj (1540) – Samugarh (1658, Dara Shikoh vs Aurangzeb and Murad Baksh).

29-013.r: Haji Begum → built Humayun's tomb, Delhi (1565-1572 A.D.); architects Mirak Mirza Ghiyash and son Sayyid Muhammad; first Mughal double dome mausoleum.

29-014.r: Silver coin (rupee) → Sher Shah; pure gold, silver and copper coins; silver rupee 178 grains (173 pure); basis of Mughal and British currency.

29-015.r: Sher Shah's currency → pure silver Rupiya (178 grains) and copper Daam (380 grains); Rupiya : Daam = 1 : 64.
29-015.h: 64 dams = 1 rupee: think of a 64-square chessboard of copper coins.

29-017.r: Sher Shah → architect of a brilliant administrative system; his qualities as ruler were MORE remarkable than his battle wins; only statement 1 true.

29-018.r: Sher Shah Suri died → May 22, 1545 AD, wounded by a gunpowder explosion during the siege of Kalinjar Fort, his last campaign.

29-020.r: 'I would have lost the empire for a handful of millet' → Sher Shah, impressed by Rajput courage in the battle of Marwar.

29-021.r: Jaita and Kumpa → generals of Maldeo Rathore of Marwar; their valour at the Battle of Sammel made Sher Shah speak of 'a few grains of bajra'.

29-022.r: Sher Shah's mausoleum → Sasaram (Rohtas, Bihar): brick tomb in the middle of a tank, a noble specimen of Afghan architecture.

29-024.r: Sher Shah (Farid Khan, son of an Afghan Jagirdar of Sasaram; 'Sher' for killing a tiger) → died 1545 A.D., buried at Sasaram.

29-025.r: Qila-i-Kuhna, Delhi (1541 A.D.) → built by Sher Shah; not Atala Masjid, Bara Sona Masjid or Quwwat-ul-Islam.

29-026.r: Purana Qila, Delhi → built by Sher Shah and Humayun; Qila-i-Kuhna mosque and Sher Mandal inside it were built by Sher Shah.

29-028.r: Purana Quila's present form → Sher Shah Suri (founder of the Sur Empire); Humayun raised its citadel.

29-029.r: Sher Shah built → Sasaram Tomb (octagonal; finished 1545 under son Islam Shah) and Qila-e-Kuhna Mosque (Purana Qila); not Sikandar's tomb or Jama Masjid.

29-030.r: 'Patta' and 'qabuliyat' → Sher Shah: patta stated the government's share; the peasant accepted it through qabuliyat.

29-031.r: Sadak-e-Azam (Grand Trunk Road) → built by Shershah Suri from Sonargaon (Bangladesh) to Kabul (Afghanistan).

29-032.r: Successor of Sher Shah → Islam Shah Suri, his second son and second ruler of the Sur Dynasty.

29-033.r: Troops in units of two hundred, two hundred fifty and five hundred → Islam Shah (ruled 8 years); Sikandar Shah continued it; hence 'more than one'.

30-001.r: Akbar enthroned → at Kalanaur, on news of Humayun's death (fell from the stairs of the Dinpanah library).

30-002.r: Bairam Khan (Akbar's guardian) → made Wazir and given the title Khan-i-Khanan at that appointment; statement 1 true, 2 false.

30-003.r: Battle of Haldighati (June 1576) → Akbar's aim: subdue Rana Pratap; Man Singh led about 5000 soldiers; Rana lost and took refuge in Aravali Hills.
